JPMorgan Chase is blocking outside AI agents from logging in to or acting on customer accounts, CEO Jamie Dimon said Tuesday, citing security risks from "rogue agents." The move puts banks and consumer AI assistants on a collision course over who controls access to financial data. BeInCrypto's latest report on the State of AI Agent Payments 2026 found that agentic payments are mostly being used for microtransactions, but not within institutions at scale. An AI agent is software that carries out tasks for a user, such as checking balances or booking travel. JPMorgan see such agents as a risk when they log in with a customer's banking credentials. "We're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company because that's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan… You don't want rogue agents," Dimon said during JPMorgan's third-quarter earnings call. JPMorgan will not let outside AI agents log in to or act on customer accounts. The bank says outside agents are too risky for clients and for JPMorgan. It blocks third-party agents that try to obtain customers' banking credentials. It still supports customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers. The stakes are high: $15.3 billion in third-quarter net income and $5.1 trillion in total assets as of Sept. 30. A Cloud Security Alliance note says a campaign used three open-source AI agents to breach at least 27 organizations. Together, these points explain why the bank is drawing a firm line. Some firms already allow them. Germany's Scalable Capital, for example, opened its platform to ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok in August. Users could analyze portfolios and place trades through prompts. However, they had to approve every trade, and the assistants could not make payments or withdraw money. Meta's Muse follows a similar model. Launched in September, it connects to financial accounts through Plaid, offering guidance on balances, transactions, and investment holdings. Retail is pushing back harder. On September 20, Amazon began blocking Muse from its site. As a result, shoppers who use it now see pop-ups saying the use violates Amazon's terms. According to Fortune, Meta declined to comment on whether Muse could keep offering financial help if more banks block outside agents. Meta is developing Poppy, a personal agent protocol with Sierra that tells companies when an agent acts for a customer. Dimon, for his part, warned that more people relying on these agents would raise the risks for banks and customers. Still, he added that JPMorgan is building its own tools to protect customers. According to The Fly, Freedom Broker lifted its rating to Buy from Hold on October 15 and nudged its price target to $370 from $365. Its reasoning was straightforward: the entry price had become more attractive. Credit costs still deserve a close look. JPMorgan's October 13 earnings release reported a $539 million net reserve addition and $2.2 billion in net charge-offs during the third quarter, bringing total credit costs to roughly $2.7 billion. The standardized common-equity Tier 1 capital ratio stood at 13.9%. The reserve addition increased the cushion for potential losses; charge-offs reflected losses already recognized. The valuation picture adds a wrinkle: shares trade 10.26% above the $309.94 GF Value estimate, suggesting the upgrade does not automatically make the stock a bargain. The reserve build accounted for roughly one-fifth of quarterly credit costs. The next test is whether lending returns can hold up without a sharper rise in provisions or actual losses. title: Eastman Chemical cut at J.P. Morgan as commodity spreads no longer favorable - TradingView
content: Eastman Chemical EMN slipped 2.6% in Friday's trading as J.P. Morgan downgraded the specialty chemicals company to Neutral from Overweight with a $66 price target, lowered from $82, saying commodity spreads are no longer favorable as propane prices rise while propylene and ethylene prices fall. The price of propane has climbed to $1.07/gal from $0.74 at the end of August, but the spot price of polymer-grade propylene has moved lower at $0.39/gal from $0.41, which took the propane-propylene spread to ~$0.02/lb from $0.11 in August, JPM analyst Jeffrey Zekauskas said, noting that Eastman EMN produces ~500M lbs of propylene and buys 500M lbs on a cost-plus basis, and the narrowing of spreads could lower annual EBITDA by $90M. Likewise, the price of ethylene has moved lower to $0.235/lb from $0.25 since the end of August, while the price of ethane rose to $0.31/gal from $0.24, cutting the ethylene spread to $0.05/lb from $0.10 at the end of August, which could shave $55M in annual EBITDA from August levels. "We had thought that operating income from the Chemical Intermediates segment could be about $130M in 2026," Zekauskas wrote. title: Inflation, Yields and Equities: When Does the Pressure Actually Matter? - J.P. Morgan
content:

Discover our approach, digital tools and community initiatives. Equities have remained resilient despite elevated inflation and higher yields. Earnings may determine how long that resilience lasts. September’s CPI report was a reminder that the path back to 2% inflation remains uneven. Headline prices rose 0.6% on the month and 3.7% from a year earlier, with the annual measure one-tenth above consensus. Energy did much of the damage: Gasoline rose 9.1% and accounted for more than half of the monthly headline increase. The September PPI reinforced the signal: Producer prices rose 1.3% in September and 6.3% from a year earlier, with both significantly hotter than expected. In response to CPI, the market initially followed the textbook: The 2-year yield rose and the curve bear-flattened – meaning yields rose across the curve, but shorter-term yields increased more than longer-term yields. Futures roughly doubled the implied probability of an October quarter-point Federal Reserve rate hike to the mid-40% range. But the move faded through the day. By Wednesday’s close, the Treasury sell-off had reversed and October hike odds had moved back below 30%. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 was only slightly lower after CPI, then weakened as the session progressed and concerns about artificial intelligence (AI)-linked companies took over. That pressure continued despite the hot PPI print, while the Treasury curve has kept flattening – but from the other direction: Long-end yields have fallen more than front-end yields in a flight-to-safety move that began on Wednesday and extended into Thursday. The line chart shows the S&P 500 index level from 1966 to 2026 on a logarithmic y‑axis (roughly 32 to 8,192), highlighting “streaks of 60+ months above CPI 2%” and indicating the other periods. Across the first qualifying inflation regime (Feb 1966–Mar 1986, 242 months), the index trends upward; in the second qualifying regime (Feb 1987–Oct 1997, 129 months) the line rises; and in the most recent qualifying regime (Mar 2021–Sep 2026, 66 months) the index climbs. However, in all the in between periods (1986-1987 and 1997-2021), the S&P 500 increases as well. Source: JPM WM Solutions. Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of September 30, 2026. Past performance is no guarantee of future results. It is not possible to invest directly in an index. Across long stretches when CPI remained above 2%, the S&P 500 still compounded meaningfully. In fact, equities have historically delivered positive long-term returns even during extended periods of above-target inflation, including the current episode. It’s not that inflation is universally good for stocks, but a level of inflation above the Fed’s target says remarkably little about long-run equity returns on its own. Inflation shocks can still create sharp near-term volatility; 2022 is a clear example. Inflation still matters over time to equity performance through changes in the policy path and discount rates, as well as pressure on real household income or corporate margins. The distinction is between a rate above 2% that is relatively targeted and an inflation process that is accelerating, broadening and becoming embedded in expectations. Equities have historically been able to live with the former. The latter is where the economic and valuation damage becomes harder to contain. Similar to inflation’s effect on equities, yield levels don’t matter as much to equities as the rate of change of yield levels. Mid- to long-end Treasury yields have hit levels not seen in about two decades, and yet equities hover near all-time highs. This line chart compares cumulative S&P 500 returns over 60 trading days for 25 historical episodes resembling the current rise in the 10-year Treasury yield; the horizontal axis shows trading days from the episode start and the vertical axis shows cumulative return, with individual historical paths, their equal-weighted average, and the current rolling 30-day episode. At the latest observation, the current episode is up 1.1% versus a historical average of 0.4%; the broad spread of event lines indicates that outcomes varied considerably across comparable periods. Source: Bloomberg Finance L.P. Data as of October 14, 2026. Note: Events are the 25 closest non-overlapping historical episodes with an equal-or-larger 30-day 10-year yield rise and policy pricing within +/-1 hike-equivalent of today. Past performance is no guarantee of future results. It is not possible to invest directly in an index. Treasury sell-offs have not produced one consistent outcome for stocks. On average, the S&P 500 response has been subdued: The historical path is soft and choppy, but only basically flat 60 trading days into the move. The individual episodes, however, are highly varied – some produced meaningful drawdowns, while others were absorbed with little lasting effect. That dispersion is the point: A bond sell-off can be a headwind, but the rates move alone does not determine the equity outcome. Inflation and yields matter most for stocks when they begin to weaken demand, compress margins, raise financing costs or force analysts to cut estimates. Until those effects show up in earnings, equities can often absorb a surprising amount of macro volatility. Credit is showing some early pressure – CCC-rated bond spreads are up more than 100 basis points this year – but it remains contained. Roughly 5.5% of the high-yield index is distressed, up from 4.4% but still well below the 11% seen in 2022. The equity sell-off over the past couple of days has also been driven by AI-linked debt concerns. Essentially, credit markets are repricing policy uncertainty, while the equity market is starting to search for evidence of fundamental damage. Earnings season is therefore an important test. The first read from the large banks was broadly resilient: lending income and market-sensitive businesses provided support, while consumer credit did not show broad deterioration. The message is not that higher rates are harmless, but that the pressure remains manageable. Market concentration may also provide a near-term buffer because the largest index weights are profitable companies with significant cash generation: Only 48% of S&P 500 constituents are trading above their 200-day moving average, down from 73% just two months ago. That narrow leadership is not necessarily healthy over the long run (as we’re seeing over the past couple of days), but it can temporarily insulate the index from weakness among companies more immediately affected by higher rates and inflation. As the rest of earnings season unfolds, the key question is whether inflation is beginning to weigh on company fundamentals. Consensus still calls for S&P 500 earnings to grow roughly 30% from a year earlier, which would mark a third consecutive quarter above 25%, while estimates actually rose during the quarter rather than following their usual downward drift. Furthermore, nine of 11 sectors are expecting double-digit earnings growth this year, including the Tech sector, which is expected to grow 64%. As long as earnings hold, equities can take hotter inflation and higher yields. If guidance starts to show weaker demand, margin pressure or rising financing costs, the same inflation data will matter much more. Equities can continue to perform as long as investors continue to see tighter policy as a manageable adjustment rather than the start of a damaging cycle, and as long as earnings continue to show resilience. The first warning would be a broader inflation process: consecutive upside core readings, stronger labor-intensive services inflation or rising market- and survey-based expectations. The second would be visible credit transmission: wider high-yield spreads, deteriorating interest coverage, rising delinquencies or tighter lending standards. The third would be a break in the earnings story through negative revisions, margin compression or weaker guidance. Inflation and bond volatility are testing the equity market and will likely remain headwinds in the near term. Equities have absorbed the pressure so far, partly because of market concentration, and could continue to grind higher as long as these risks remain familiar and earnings bolster confidence. title: JP Morgan deepens critical minerals push - The National
content: JP Morgan has appointed an executive to lead the company's critical mineral efforts under its $1.5 trillion drive to invest in industries deemed significant to US national economic security. Andrew Frame will oversee the Security and Resilience Initiative's critical minerals strategy across extraction, refining and processing, a company representative confirmed to The National. Mr Frame's mandate will centre on addressing bottlenecks across the value chain for an industry considered essential to advanced manufacturing, energy and defence, they said. Mr Frame's appointment was first reported by Mining.com. Companies at core of US push to break China's rare-earth grip locked in legal row JP Morgan launched its 10-year, $1.5 trillion Security and Resiliency Initiative last year. The drive spans four sectors – supply chain and advanced manufacturing, defence and aerospace, energy independence and resilience, and frontier and strategic technology. The bank said those are then divided into 27 subsections ranging from fishing to critical defence components. Critical minerals fall under the supply chain and advanced manufacturing category, while battery storage and grid resilience fall under defence and aerospace. Artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and quantum computing make up the initiative's frontier strategies sector. The $1.5 trillion builds on the previously announced $1 trillion the company planned to finance over the next decade. The commitment includes a separate $10 billion allocation for direct equity investments. “It has become painfully clear that the United States has allowed itself to become too reliant on unreliable sources of critical minerals, products and manufacturing – all of which are essential for our national security,” JP Morgan chief executive Jamie Dimon said. Mr Dimon told analysts during the company's third-quarter earnings call this week that the company “probably” deployed more than $200 billion in the first year. Mr Frame's appointment makes him an integral part of the US critical minerals push amid a string of private and federal capital injection into the sector to strengthen the country's supply chain. Since 2025, the US government has announced $10.8 billion in investments, including $5.1 billion in total private capital, in 14 critical minerals companies, using a range of tools from equity stakes to grants, loans and offtake agreements, according to the Council of Foreign Relations. In September, Houston-based start-up Hertha Metals said it had closed a $133.65 million Series A round that includes a $65 million equity investment from the Pentagon. The company is planning on producing high-purity iron for rare-earth magnets needed for F-35 fighter jets and missile-guidance systems. The US government also holds equity stakes in companies across the critical minerals supply chain including MP Materials, USA Rare Earth, and Canada-based Lithium Americas. Also in September, Glencore and Mercuria became the first two companies to participate in VaultCo, a public-private partnership designed to implement the administration's Project Vault initiative. Glencore said its $500 million commitment from Export-Import Bank will allow it to create a critical minerals reserve in the US. Mercuria also announced a $500 million commitment, bringing the total pledge from the companies to $1 billion. “Mineral security is national security. VaultCo is working to ensure the US industrial base has access to the critical minerals needed to build the products everyday Americans rely on and lead the world when they need it most,” ValtCo executive chair Brett Lambert said. Dimon noted, however, that activity was already moderating in the third quarter. The third quarter was bound to see a slowdown from the second quarter, which featured the Space Exploration Technologies initial public offering (IPO), the biggest IPO ever. In the commercial and investment banking (CIB) segment, JPMorgan Chase's revenue increased 14% year over year, but it was down 8% from last quarter. The company had already signaled the slowdown at the Barclays Global Financial Services Conference in September, when Co-President Doug Petno said that the company expected a mid-teens increase, and the stock dropped at the time. "Large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising interest rates and geopolitical conditions continue to shift under the surface," he said. He ended on a positive note, pointing out that "these forces may be manageable, but we remain prepared for a wide range of outcomes." Each of these factors alone could have a major impact on the economy. The U.S. debt has reached $40.25 trillion and continues to rise, while many global regions are dealing with spiraling deficits. Inflation is still raging, aided in part by the resilient U.S. consumer, but it isn't likely to stay that way forever. Interest rates also slow the economy and specifically impact banks because fewer people look for loans when interest rates are high, both personally and commercially, and default rates rise. title: J.P. Morgan Payments Powers Mercado Libre’s Global Selling Expansion - Financial IT
content: Cross-border marketplace flows can introduce complexity across onboarding, funding movement, and seller pay-outs—especially when programs expand quickly across geographies. For marketplaces, embedded payments can streamline complex multi-party cross-border transactions, simplify payment operations, and improve the seller experience. Mercado Libre, the leading e-commerce platform based in Latin America, selected J.P. Morgan Payments to support the continued growth of its Global Selling program, which enables U.S.-based businesses to sell across Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Uruguay. By leveraging our Embedded Payments solution, Mercado Libre can streamline cross-border payments and accelerate onboarding to J.P. Morgan Payments deposit services for eligible U.S. sellers as the program continues to scale. “J.P. Morgan Payments brought the global scale, security and infrastructure we needed to support cross-border fund flows between Latin America and the U.S.,” said Gregorio Bekes, Financial Planning & Treasury Senior Vice President at Mercado Libre. “By creating an integrated experience for onboarding and cross-border payment management within our platform, this collaboration is helping us streamline payment operations and support the continued growth of our Global Selling program.” Our Embedded Payments solution helps accelerate sellers’ setup for payments and financial services and makes it easier for sellers to receive and manage funds across borders. In an initial pilot, Mercado Libre onboarded U.S. sellers to J.P. Morgan Payments using our embedded Know Your Customer (KYC) and Know Your Business (KYB) capabilities, reducing friction in the financial-services onboarding process and helping speed time to activation. Mercado Libre is also leveraging our ability to receive bulk cross-border payments through ACH payouts infrastructure, helping move marketplace funds from Latin America to U.S. sellers. "We’re excited to support Mercado Libre’s well-established platform to simplify their client and customer experience with the expertise, security and resilience we are known for,” said Ryan Schmiedl, Global Head of Embedded Finance & Solutions at J.P. Morgan Payments. “Marketplace sellers can keep their whole experience within Mercado Libre’s platform, from opening a bank account to receiving and moving funds from sales proceeds, for a frictionless end-to-end solution.” Hear more at leading industry conference Money20/20 2026 in Las Vegas, Oct. 18-21, during the "When Fraudsters Adapt, Security Adapts: Prevention for Embedded Finance" session featuring leaders from Mercado Libre, BILL, Walmart and J.P. Morgan Payments on how platforms and merchants balance embedded experiences with robust, adaptive security. title: Investing in venture capital and growth equity today - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Venture capital and growth equity are at an inflection point. After a bruising multi-year correction, the setup today looks increasingly compelling: Value creation is migrating into private markets at precisely the moment of a generational technology shift, capital markets are reopening across every major exit channel, and distributions are poised to inflect after years of drought. The opportunity is real, but it is uneven. We believe returns will concentrate among a narrow set of winners and top-tier managers, which makes disciplined portfolio construction and manager selection the decisive levers. In what follows, we lay out what venture capital and growth equity actually are, why the environment is compelling today, where the opportunities lie (e.g., artificial intelligence, security), what accelerating capital markets activity means for distributions and sentiment, and think about implementation and allocation. Consider this our roadmap for investors seeking to navigate one of the most dynamic periods in private markets in recent memory. Venture capital and growth equity invest in private companies at different stages of maturity. Venture capital targets early-stage companies where the business model is unproven and risk is highest. Growth equity focuses on mid- to late-stage companies with established product-market fit, demonstrated revenue traction and clear paths to market leadership. Together, they capture innovation from earliest inception through to public-market access—or, increasingly, indefinite private status. The distinction matters. Early-stage venture is front-loaded in risk and back-loaded in returns, driven by a handful of outsized winners across many investments. Growth equity targets more de-risked models with higher revenue visibility and nearer-term liquidity. Both share a critical trait: access to high-growth innovation increasingly unavailable in public markets. As companies stay private longer amid a generational technological shift, these strategies capture economic growth that public-only portfolios structurally miss. This is not simply return enhancement; it is about adding access points to innovation that can’t be accessed in public markets. We became more constructive early last year. Three reinforcing forces drove that shift: the structural migration of value creation into private markets, the acceleration of secular growth themes (AI, healthcare, defense) and revitalization in exit channels across M&A, IPOs and GP-led secondaries. This resurgence is structural, not cyclical. Innovative companies increasingly spend their growth phase in private hands. Meanwhile, attractive entry points are emerging in early-stage venture, where valuations have been more insulated than late-stage names now dominated by LLM leaders. Companies staying private for longer, creating significant value Companies with the size and scale to IPO are staying private longer, creating meaningful value in the private markets. There are four reasons for this in our view: We see artificial intelligence not as a sector-specific theme but as a broad-based force for innovation affecting nearly every industry. The defining shift is from “software as a service” to “services as software.” This transition could represent a ~$6 trillion opportunity by decade-end as AI disrupts segments of the services industry. Promising sub-sectors, in our view, include: The access point for this opportunity is overwhelmingly in VC and growth equity, given that the vast majority of software companies remain private through their highest-growth phase. More than tech: Finding opportunities in healthcare, evolving definition of security Venture capital and growth equity’s enduring appeal lies in their ability to capture long-term secular themes that are underrepresented or inaccessible in public markets. AI is a major theme, but we believe the opportunity is larger than that. Innovation in healthcare (drug engineering, digital health) and security represent robust multi-year growth themes. A common question we get is, given the valuation increases we have seen in later-stage venture, is it too late? Parsing through venture further, the current environment suggests a thoughtful balance between early- and late-stage exposure may be warranted, with early-stage venture offering a particularly interesting risk/reward profile given where late-stage valuations sit today. A couple of supporting points: Bottom line: A well-constructed venture allocation may benefit from exposure across stages, capturing the liquidity and de-risking advantages of late-stage while leaning into the alpha potential and valuation insulation that early-stage can offer. In today's environment, tilting toward smaller-cap, early-stage managers may represent an attractive way to enhance return potential without fully concentrating late-stage valuation risk. Global capital markets activity is surging. M&A volumes are up roughly 45% year-over-year to about ＄3.5 trillion year-to-date, IPO issuance is on pace to exceed ＄200 billion in 2026 (approaching 2021 levels),6 and GP-led secondaries continue their multi-year climb. If these trends hold, 2026 could surpass 2021 as the biggest capital markets year of the past decade. The exit machinery (M&A, IPOs and secondaries) is clearly on the upswing, a welcome shift for an asset class that has run below-average distributions for years. A handful of mega-IPOs are poised to validate the public listing route for two cohorts: thematically oriented companies in AI and defense/security and high-quality, profitable businesses with the scale and franchise value to command public-market interest. But these listings are unlikely to open the floodgates broadly. Companies that fall short on size, thematic relevance or profitability will keep exiting through alternative channels: GP-led secondaries, continuation vehicles, sponsor-to-sponsor deals and strategic M&A. Critically, mega-IPOs could just as easily monopolize capital and crowd out smaller listings, reinforcing rather than undermining the "private for longer" thesis. The alternative exit ecosystem is here to stay: 2025 secondary volumes exceeded ＄240 billion (up 48% year-over-year), the GP-led market reached ＄115 billion and has compounded at roughly 30% annually since 2017, and single-asset continuation vehicles surged from ＄2 billion in 2018 to ＄31 billion in 2024, the fastest-growing segment of the secondary market.7 VC secondaries are gaining traction too. These options keep the private-for-longer dynamic structurally intact even as the IPO window reopens. The distribution picture is turning. Goldman Sachs estimates roughly ＄500 billion in stock could become eligible for sale in 2026; assuming about 25% is venture-held, that implies an estimated ＄125 billion in potential VC distributions over the next 12 to 24 months, the largest wave since 2021.8 With broader M&A and secondary momentum, industry cash flows could flip positive within a couple of years. But the benefits will be strikingly uneven. More than 70% of first-quarter 2026 deal value accrued to just five managers, and the spread between top- and bottom-quartile VC returns exceeds 30 percentage points in most vintage years, roughly three times wider than buyout.9 IPOs have historically been a more typical VC exit than buyout, so as mega-IPOs come to market, DPI and realized returns should improve in VC and growth equity, but the gains will concentrate among a narrow set of GPs with early access to category leaders in key themes. Overall, capital markets are reopening across M&A, IPOs and GP-led secondaries, and distributions are set to inflect after years of drought. But the opportunity is deeply uneven: Returns may concentrate among a narrow set of category-leading companies and top-tier managers. Mega-IPOs may generate meaningful liquidity without negating the private-for-longer thesis, as alternative exit channels are too mature and too essential to be displaced. For limited partners, the implication is clear: Disciplined portfolio construction and rigorous manager selection are the decisive levers for capturing this cycle’s gains. Performance dispersion is exceptionally wide, with the gap between top- and bottom-quartile managers greater in venture than in any other alternatives category, which makes access to top-tier managers critical. And because outcomes are driven by a small number of investments that are difficult to predict in advance, committing consistently across vintages improves the odds of participating in the few that drive the majority of long-term returns. For qualified investors, it may be prudent to consider strategic allocations to venture capital and growth equity. With the potential for outsize returns to be concentrated among top managers, thoughtful selection and disciplined investment are critical to capturing what we expect to be the asset class’s resurgence. title: Specialty lending: The ballast in uncertain markets - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. The superyacht market has no reason to be this steady. Rates have moved sharply, energy prices have swung and the macro backdrop looks meaningfully different from where it was at the start of the year. And yet, order books at the leading shipyards remain full, secondary market pricing has held and the conversations taking place around Monaco, Port Hercules continue as they always do. The question, then, is not whether the yacht market can absorb uncertainty; but rather, are buyers’ financing strategies as equally resilient? The world that owners and buyers are navigating is not the one they anticipated. Rate expectations have swung from cuts to potential hikes, and geopolitical tensions have unsettled energy markets. The first half of 2026 was defined largely by events in the Middle East, which sent energy prices spike higher. In a year of shifting narratives, attention has moved to monetary policy, where the tone has grown more hawkish than most expected. The story the market was telling in January is not the one it is telling now, and has yet to settle. This is not an environment that rewards complacency, and for superyacht owners and prospective buyers, the tension between confidence and caution is likely to shape how capital gets deployed in the months ahead. Complexity has a way of surfacing questions that calmer conditions allow people to defer. Investors will have to consider whether a financing structure has the flexibility to support broader portfolio goals — and if it can hold its shape should conditions shift again. The outlook for the superyacht market remains constructive, and this strength is structural rather than accidental. Order books at the most established shipyards extend years into the future, and that supply constraint has continued to put a floor under secondary market pricing — even as other asset classes have felt the pressure of a more volatile environment. Geopolitical uncertainty and energy price instability have not materially disrupted demand at this level of the market, and the evidence from this year suggests they are unlikely to. For buyers seeking a more immediate path to ownership, the pre-owned market offers a direct and often well-priced route. Alternatively, for those drawn to commissioning their own specifications, new builds remain available on the right timeline. However, the takeaway should be that while conditions are durable, diligent consideration should still be given to the surrounding financial mechanism of any purchase. A thoughtful approach is one that makes ownership more robust and better aligned with the broader portfolio goals that a year like this one tends to bring into focus. When rates fall, clients can capitalise on lower-cost leverage and redeploy capital toward new opportunities. When rates rise, locking in long-term fixed financing on a durable physical asset provides payment certainty and a meaningful buffer against further increases. The structure, if engineered carefully from the outset, performs across both environments rather than becoming a liability when conditions shift. For non-euro clients, currency exposure adds a further dimension that too often enters the conversation late. With the world's leading shipyards concentrated in Europe, recent dollar movements have made hedging a necessary component of any comprehensive financing structure, not a refinement to be addressed once contracts are signed. More broadly, the logic of yacht financing rests on preserving liquidity and maintaining optionality: avoiding the concentration of capital in a single asset and keeping flexibility intact across a broader portfolio. Some clients want a partner to navigate the complexity of a major build alongside them, whereas others are focused on keeping their broader investment architecture intact. A structure designed carefully from the outset serves both, and throughout periods of uncertainty as we have recently seen, that adaptability is paramount. Uncertainty is a reason to structure well, not to wait. Our conversations with clients begin with a single question: What should your wealth accomplish, and how does yacht financing fit within that picture? When that question is answered clearly, the asset supports the plan rather than complicating it. After all, the seas are often rough. The point is to be built to weather the storm. In uncertain markets, specialty lending prices risk by focusing on durability and flexibility: the underlying asset’s resilience (e.g., a durable physical asset), payment certainty through long-term fixed financing when appropriate, and structures that can “hold their shape” if rates or narratives shift again. Lenders navigate changing markets by anticipating shifting narratives (rates, geopolitics, energy) and building adaptable specialty lending structures early — addressing interest-rate strategy up front and, for non-euro clients, integrating currency hedging as a core component rather than a late-stage add-on. The protections that matter most are those that preserve resilience and clarity under volatility: payment certainty (often via long-term fixed-rate structures), disciplined up-front structuring to avoid surprises later, and safeguards that keep broader portfolio flexibility intact rather than concentrating capital in a single asset. Superyacht financing adds market- and execution-specific risks: long timelines for new builds, reliance on shipyard schedules, and — especially for non-euro clients — meaningful currency exposure because leading shipyards are concentrated in Europe, making hedging a necessary part of a comprehensive structure. The superyacht market has held its course for structural reasons: leading shipyards’ order books extend years out, constraining supply and putting a floor under secondary market pricing, while this year’s geopolitical and energy volatility has not materially disrupted demand at the top end. Master trust filings are the monthly window into securitised credit card performance, and a sequential decline in net charge-offs of this size sits within the normal range of month-to-month variation rather than marking a trend break on its own. Historically the card charge-off series has been one of the cleaner real-time reads on the consumer, with deterioration tending to show first in delinquencies before feeding through to charge-offs with a lag of a few months, so the delinquency line in the same filing is the more forward-looking tell. A single month's improvement after a stretch of rising loss rates has, in past cycles, often proved to be noise rather than inflection; the pattern that matters is several consecutive prints moving together across issuers, since idiosyncratic portfolio mix and seasonal factors can move one trust independently of the cohort. For the large card issuers this series is read against the pace of reserve builds and the guidance embedded in card revenue, rather than against the quarter's headline numbers. The follow-ons are the comparable monthly trust filings from the peer card issuers and the next round of delinquency data, which together separate issuer-specific movement from a genuine turn in consumer credit.

title: JPMorgan Chase (JPM) Stock Faces Rising Costs Despite Profit Strength - Simply Wall Street
content:
The market barely flinched. JPMorgan Chase shares edged about 1% higher into the print, even as the bank dropped a heavy Q3 earnings package that mixed solid profitability with rising cost pressure. Headline profit of US$15.3b and earnings per share of US$5.57 reminded investors why this stock carries a premium P/E to the banking sector. The sharper sting came from expenses of US$27.3b, which pulled the cost to income ratio to 54% and put the spotlight squarely on whether this profit engine is facing the beginnings of a margin squeeze. Is JPMorgan Chase a premium bank that still trades at a discount, or has the market already priced in the best of this profit story? Bulls argue JPMorgan Chase can compound earnings through fee rich wealth, payments and card growth while funding long dated projects like the Security & Resiliency Initiative without sacrificing profitability. Q3 results offer several proof points. Asset & Wealth Management delivered US$6.9b of revenue with a 36% pretax margin, US$51b of long term net inflows and AUM of US$5.2t. That combination of fresh money and high margins fits the thesis that fee income can do more of the heavy lifting over time. Consumer & Community Banking adds support. Revenue of US$21.2b, 10% card and debit spend growth, 4% deposit growth and about 650,000 new checking accounts show the franchise still attracts everyday customers. Client investment assets of US$1.4t, up 15%, link the consumer bank directly into the wealth funnel, which is exactly the flywheel bulls have been looking for. Skeptics focus on rising costs, late cycle credit risk and reliance on strong markets. Q3 gives them some evidence. Group expenses of US$27.3b rose faster than revenue and pulled the cost to income ratio to 54%. Management now flags Q4 expenses around US$27.5b and an early view that 2027 costs could sit near US$114b. That tilts the debate toward whether AI and tech spending are eroding margin while benefits stay vague. Credit costs of US$2.7b, including a US$539m reserve build, signal a cautious stance on future losses even as card net charge off guidance sits near 3.2%. In the Corporate & Investment Bank, revenue of US$22.7b grew, but FICC trading fell while management already sees some activity cooling. The stock’s roughly 4% decline over 30 days suggests investors are not treating this as a clean beat and raise story. An IPO can be a defining milestone, often bringing new opportunities alongside increased financial complexity and the need for more intentional planning. For many individuals, it’s also a moment to clarify what they want their wealth to do: support causes and communities they care about, create a legacy, educate and communicate with younger generations, and align resources with long-term priorities. It can be tempting to jump straight into tactics—selecting a structure, selecting a gift amount and choosing organizations. But often, it’s helpful to first step back and view these decisions in the context of your overall vision and values, helping to position your giving strategy for long-term success. To determine if a more structured philanthropic approach makes sense for you, we recommend starting with three key questions outlined below. Philanthropy is personal. Creating a durable plan typically starts by defining what you want your giving to represent—now and over time. This can be a solo exercise, or something you choose to share with a spouse, partner or other trusted stakeholders. These themes will help bring your goals into focus. Your choice of charitable structure—which may vary by jurisdiction—is an important factor in your ability to meet your financial goals, desired involvement, privacy preferences and administrative tolerance. Over time, many philanthropic approaches evolve as needs become more complex and the scope of philanthropic ambition expands. When choosing a vehicle, first clarify your decision-making and operating preferences: If you choose to involve others, a well-defined decision-making process will help ensure that your giving is efficient, consistent and aligned with your objectives. For donors with international interests, it is also important to consider where you are tax resident, where intended recipients are located, whether gifts will cross national borders,  and which reporting and governance requirements apply. Gifts made directly to eligible charitable or nonprofit organizations, as defined under applicable local law.
Benefits: Simplicity; minimal ongoing administration.
Considerations: Less built-in structure for a sustained or multi-year strategy; coordination and recordkeeping can become more complex as giving grows. Where available, a charitable account sponsored by an eligible charitable organization that you fund, and from which you may recommend grants over time.
Benefits: Depending on local law, a DAF or similar structure may allow you to separate the timing of funding from the timing of grantmaking. This approach can be helpful if you want to contribute in a particular year while taking more time to evaluate organizations and define an impact plan. It may also offer administrative simplicity and privacy options.
Considerations: Availability, tax treatment, grant recommendations, investment choices and other features vary by jurisdiction and sponsoring organization. A standalone charitable entity, typically established or supported by a donor and often accompanied by a board and formal governance. Depending on the jurisdiction, trusts, foundations or other vehicles may be tailored to specific philanthropic and planning objectives.
Benefits: Available structures may align charitable goals with timing preferences and broader planning needs, depending on local law and individual circumstances. These often provide the donor with a higher degree of control over charitable strategy and governance.
Considerations: These structures can be complex and may be difficult to change once established; they require careful design and coordination with local legal, tax and other professional advisers. They may involve greater administrative responsibility, recordkeeping, operating costs and formal compliance and governance requirements. Many donors combine approaches—for example, direct gifts for immediate priorities plus a DAF or foundation for longer-term giving. This is often the most practical course of action. As you evaluate options, it helps to assess your current state and cost: how giving is currently managed, which functions are handled directly versus outsourced, whether existing advisors coordinate effectively, whether existing technology meets your needs and the expected startup and ongoing operating costs. It is also important to consider applicable legal, tax, regulatory, reporting and governance requirements in each relevant jurisdiction and to seek appropriate local professional advice. After an IPO, the particular assets you donate, and the timing of those gifts, can matter as much as the vehicle you choose. Some donors prefer to give cash. Others may consider donating securities or more complex assets, depending on their goals and constraints. If planning to donate on a global basis, donors should consider whether and how contributions to a foreign charity are eligible for a charitable deduction in their country of residence. Donors should also consider foreign exchange and currency matters and cross-border reporting and disclosure requirements. Timing can be especially important after an IPO, when income may be elevated and portfolios are being adjusted. Depending on local tax rules and the timing of the sale of shares, donors may consider accelerating or combining planned gifts into a particular tax year, or if spreading gifts over time may be more appropriate. A local tax advisor can help you choose an approach that fits your circumstances. You’ll want to take inventory of your capital and commitments—what you own, the levels of concentration and liquidity, and the priorities that need to be funded. This will help you align your assets with your giving plan, timing preferences and implementation realities. If you plan to donate company shares or other equity interests, you’ll want to coordinate the timing of your donation with the implementation of your broader diversification approach, any applicable transfer restrictions and the legal and tax rules in relevant jurisdictions. Because available structures have different tax attributes and regulatory considerations across jurisdictions, it’s important to approach asset selection deliberately and in coordination with appropriate local legal, tax and other professional advisors. Philanthropic planning is an ongoing process that will evolve alongside your needs, market conditions and long-term objectives. Understanding your motivations, the giving vehicles available to you and the best timing for your gifts are excellent foundations for managing your philanthropic impact. Your J.P. Management pointed to strong consumer spending, healthy deposit growth, and robust asset and wealth management inflows as key drivers, while acknowledging that markets revenue was mixed and expenses rose due to wage inflation and front office hiring. CEO Jamie Dimon cited the firm's ability to grow its customer base and maintain its leadership in retail deposit share, stating, "We retained our number 1 position in retail deposit share based on FDIC data." Looking forward, management highlighted a constructive but uncertain outlook, with a focus on navigating a dynamic macroeconomic environment and ongoing investment in technology and risk management. CFO Jeremy Barnum indicated that net interest income guidance is supported by continued balance sheet growth and moderate rate sensitivity, but cautioned that expense projections remain fluid due to discretionary investments and the evolving impact of artificial intelligence initiatives. Dimon emphasized, "The world needs capital, and we believe we can redeploy that capital at very good returns over time." Management attributed the quarter's performance to resilient consumer and business banking, continued investment, and strong asset management flows, but cited higher expenses and some market-related headwinds. Consumer banking momentum: The Chase Consumer & Community Banking segment benefited from higher card spending and deposit growth, with management noting 10% year-over-year growth in debit and credit card spend and a strong pace of new checking account openings. Asset management inflows: The Asset and Wealth Management division saw net inflows driven by fixed income products and favorable market levels, leading to a 15% increase in client investment assets year-over-year. Mixed markets revenue: Markets revenue was uneven, with equities trading up 49% but fixed income, commodities, and credit trading down, reflecting client demand for capital and ongoing volatility. Expense growth: Expenses rose 12% year-over-year, attributed to higher client activity, wage inflation, and hiring across front office positions, as well as continued investment in technology and compliance. Capital deployment strategy: Management reiterated a preference for reinvesting excess capital into organic business growth and security resilience initiatives rather than large-scale share repurchases, given evolving regulatory requirements and attractive returns on new investments. JPMorgan Chase's outlook depends on stable consumer trends, prudent investment, and balancing growth with disciplined expense management. Net interest income trends: Management's guidance for net interest income (NII) relies on moderate consumer and wholesale deposit growth, a stable yield curve, and ongoing loan demand. The company remains asset sensitive, meaning changes in interest rates can significantly affect NII, and current projections are built on assumptions of continued economic resilience. Expense discipline and investment: While expense guidance remains close to consensus, management stressed that actual spending will depend on discretionary investment decisions, especially around technology and artificial intelligence. The evolving competitive landscape and regulatory developments could further influence cost trajectories and capital allocation. Credit and consumer health: The resilience of consumer credit quality and stable corporate credit outlook are central to future performance. Management warned that a prolonged period of high interest rates or rising unemployment could eventually pressure consumer credit, while corporate credit remains stable but subject to sector-specific challenges such as energy prices and commercial real estate. Looking ahead, the StockStory team will be monitoring (1) the pace and sustainability of consumer deposit and card spending growth, (2) management's ability to control expense inflation amid continued investment, and (3) progress in translating artificial intelligence initiatives into visible productivity or revenue gains. title: JPM, Citi, Wells Fargo Or Goldman Sachs: Which Big Bank Is The Better Buy After Q3 Results? - TradingView
content: Third-quarter earnings season kicked off Tuesday, with big banks reporting results. Goldman Sachs (GS), Citigroup (C), Wells Fargo (WFC) and JPMorgan Chase (JPM) posted their prints, with shares of all closing in the red with results “a little bit disappointing” for a market that was “anticipating much better,” Gina Martin Adams, chief market strategist with HB Wealth, told Reuters. Goldman Sachs reported net revenue of $18.68 billion and earnings per share of $17.01, beating estimates. Net profit rose 29% to $5.29 billion. A 72% surge in equities revenue and a 21% increase in investment banking fees drove growth. Citigroup’s net income rose 40% year-over-year to $5.25 billion, or $2.85 per share, while revenue increased 8% to $23.85 billion. Growth in services, wealth management and investment banking supported its performance, while trading revenue declined sequentially and higher rewards and loan-loss provisions pressured credit card profitability. Wells Fargo posted total revenue of $21.87 billion, up 2% year-over-year, and profit of $5.95 billion, or $1.87 per share, beating EPS estimates but missing revenue forecasts. Average loans and deposits each grew 11%, but higher provisions for credit losses and weaker-than-expected revenue weighed on results. The bank expects fourth-quarter net interest income of about $13 billion and full-year 2026 net interest income of roughly $50 billion. JPMorgan Chase reported revenue of $50.17 billion, up 8% year-over-year, and $15.3 billion in net income, or $5.57 per share, posting a rare miss from consensus estimates. Equity trading revenue surged 49%, investment banking fees rose 14%, while fixed-income revenue fell 4%. Credit costs reached $2.7 billion. The bank raised its 2026 net interest income outlook to $106.2 billion and projected approximately $107 billion for 2027. Three American banks set new highs for interest earned from lending even as benchmark interest rates rose and pushed up borrowing costs. JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup and Wells Fargo on Tuesday reported a combined $56.5 billion of net interest income for the third quarter. JPMorgan Chase reported net interest income of about $27.1 billion, up 13% year over year, and raised its full-year 2026 forecast to $106.2 billion, with a preliminary outlook of $107 billion for 2027. Citigroup’s net interest income increased 14% year-over-year to $17 billion, supported by growth in lending and deposits. Wells Fargo’s net interest income rose 5% to $12.52 billion, driven by higher loan and investment securities balances. It now expects about $13 billion in the fourth quarter and roughly $50 billion for full-year 2026. Goldman Sachs, meanwhile, reported net interest income of $3.77 billion, down 2%, as interest expense grew faster than interest income. Goldman Sachs lowered its price targets on JPM, WFC and C stocks while maintaining ‘Buy’ ratings on all three following their Q3 earnings, according to The Fly. Goldman cut JPM’s target to $392 from $398 after the earnings miss but noted that 2027 guidance implies a $4 billion upside in pre-provision net revenue. JPMorgan is prioritizing organic balance-sheet growth and attractive capital deployment over buybacks, supported by stronger-than-expected consumer and wholesale deposit trends, including data-center financing, the analyst said. For Wells Fargo, Goldman reduced its target to $94 from $96, citing a net interest income miss driven by softer average earning-asset metrics. However, the bank continues to gain market share in capital-markets businesses as investments in its franchise pay off, it said. For Citi, Goldman lowered its target to $155 from $156 despite an earnings beat. Citi raised its 2026 net interest income guidance excluding Markets, while the bank attributed the negative share-price reaction primarily to positioning, noting that Citi had outperformed peers by two percentage points in the week before earnings. Savers are exposing themselves to major financial risks by allowing AI bots to manage their money, the boss of JP Morgan has warned. Jamie Dimon, the Wall Street chief executive, said the growing use of autonomous agents to help people with their finances was a problem if the bots got things wrong. Mr Dimon said customers could end up being liable for mistakes made by any agent acting on their behalf. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," he said. "We have to make sure we protect our customers in the right kind of way. "We will be building tools to do that too. In the meantime, we're not going to allow just any outside agent to come in inside the company because that's just too risky for clients and for JP Morgan." The warning from Wall Street puts it into direct conflict with Silicon Valley, which has pushed AI bots as a way to help people with their finances. OpenAI's ChatGPT announced a "personal finance experience" for the chatbot's paid users in the US several months ago. The tool allows customers to securely connect their financial accounts, see a dashboard of where their money is going and ask ChatGPT questions based on their own finances. Anthropic is also reportedly testing a similar feature, called Claude Money. More than half of consumers in the UK already use AI tools and a quarter use the technology for financial tasks at least once a month, according to a survey by McKinsey. That figure rises to 59pc among high-income consumers. There are also increasing concerns that AI could lead to a rapid run on a bank, as agents make it even easier to move cash from one bank to another. The technology could also hit banks' profits as AI bots move customers' cash out of zero-interest current accounts in search of better returns. Savers could shift up to £700bn out of accounts that offer little or no returns and into savings products on the advice of AI chatbots in the UK, according to consultants at McKinsey. If just 5pc to 10pc of bank balances are moved this way, the profits lenders make on deposits could drop by a fifth or more. Mr Dimon said that in the future banks would adjust to new ways of making money, perhaps through subscriptions or other services. However, he added that there was more risk in the short term, as AI agents are let loose on the financial sector. "Should regulators be thinking about what they're going to do with some of these things? Yeah, of course they should," Mr Dimon said. "It's a new world and with all these bots and agents, could someone ... cause a problem? Maybe." The warning came as JP Morgan reported a rare miss on profit in the third quarter of the year, as its bond trading revenue dropped by 4pc year-on-year. Total trading revenue was $10.3bn for the period, below Wall Street expectations of $10.5bn. Goldman Sachs also saw a small 1pc drop in bond trading to $3.47bn, significantly lower than expected.
